name: MalKamak
iocPatterns: Heartbeat polling every 2 seconds to cloud storage
Usage of rar.exe for data staging
Domain labels involving ms-tech[].us and whynooneistherefornoneofthem[].com
keyCapabilities: Command and Control (C2) via cloud services
Lateral Movement via WMI and PAExec
recommendedActions: Block known MalKamak infrastructure domains including whynooneistherefornoneofthem.com and ms-tech.us.
Monitor network traffic for high-frequency polling to Dropbox API from non-standard processes.
Alert on the creation of system services with names resembling 'Windows Defender Update' or 'nhdService'.
Conduct EDR monitoring for lsass.exe memory dumping into unknown file types like .bin.
Identify and block the use of PAExec or other modified PsExec clones across the internal network.
Filter network traffic to known threat-related domains at the perimeter.
Audit system logs for usage of csvde.exe in abnormal contexts.
Implement alert rules for automated data compression (WinRar) into files with .exe names during the exfiltration phase.
campaignsText: MalKamak is heavily associated with the 'Operation GhostShell' campaign, which has been active since at least 2017/2018 targeting defense and telecom sectors. The actor displays a consistent operational tempo, frequently updating their malware toolkit to include more advanced evasion techniques as seen in the transition to Dropbox-based C2 infrastructure in 2021. They have also been linked to broader Iranian campaigns involving the theft of aerospace data from international firms.
description: MalKamak is an Iranian-linked state-sponsored threat actor, also known as APT39 or Chafer APT, specializing in cyberespionage against aerospace and telecommunications sectors. The group utilizes highly sophisticated malware, notably the ShellClient RAT, which employs advanced evasion techniques like 'cold file' logic via Dropbox to blend into legitimate cloud traffic.
goals: The actor's primary objectives are state-sponsored espionage and intellectual property theft related to aerospace technology, telecommunications infrastructure, and defense research. They target a wide range of geographic regions including the US, Russia, and various countries in the Middle East. Their targeting strategy involves identifying specific organizations within these high-priority industries to facilitate long-term surveillance and data collection.
